receipt.public_excerpt: Despite its capabilities, GPT‑4 has similar limitations as earlier GPT models. Most importantly, it still is not fully reliable (it “hallucinates” facts and makes reasoning errors).

evidence_items.explanation: The developer of the leading model said GPT-4 has the same limits as earlier models and still hallucinates facts and makes reasoning errors. This supports the claim that the problem persisted.

receipt.public_excerpt: At the other end of the table, two Google LLMs fared much worse. A hallucination rate of over 27% for Google Palm-Chat suggests that its factual summaries of reference material are judged unreliable at best.

evidence_items.explanation: Vectara's November 2023 leaderboard found every tested LLM added unsupported facts even on a simple summarization task, with one major model above 27%. This supports the claim that hallucinations were still common across models.

receipt.public_excerpt: law firm Levidow, Levidow & Oberman got in trouble after they “submitted non-existent judicial opinions with fake quotes and citations created by the artificial intelligence tool ChatGPT.”

evidence_items.explanation: A widely reported 2023 case where ChatGPT invented court decisions. It fits the claim of serious, embarrassing errors. The report is dated November 2023; the court case itself happened earlier in 2023.

receipt.public_excerpt: While still a real issue, GPT‑4 significantly reduces hallucinations relative to previous models (which have themselves been improving with each iteration).

evidence_items.explanation: OpenAI reported measurable reductions in hallucination, which cuts against 'not a lot has changed'. It also calls hallucination 'still a real issue', which fits the core claim.

unresolved_gaps: No standard benchmark measured the same models' hallucination rates in both March 2022 and November 2023, so 'not a lot has changed' cannot be measured directly.
'Rampant' has no threshold; GPT-4's 3% rate on Vectara's summarization test could be read either way.
